market_context: United States/general English; rinsing canned beans, sodium reduction and uses for packing liquid
title: Should you rinse canned beans?

seo.title: Should you rinse canned beans?
seo.meta_description: Rinsing is optional. It helps reduce sodium and packing-liquid flavor; one study found 36% less sodium after draining and 41% less after draining plus rinsing.
seo.search_intent: Learn when canned beans should be rinsed, how much sodium rinsing removes and when the liquid can be useful.

excerpt: You do not have to rinse canned beans for safety. Rinsing is useful when you want less sodium or less packing-liquid flavor: one study found a 36% sodium reduction after draining and 41% after draining plus rinsing.
content_html:
Opening a can, pouring the beans into a colander and rinsing them is common, but rinsing is not a food-safety requirement. Canned beans are already cooked. Rinsing mainly changes sodium, flavor, surface starch and how much packing liquid enters the recipe.

Rinsing helps when sodium is the goal

A study of several brands and five bean types found that draining for two minutes lowered average sodium from 503 to 321 mg per label serving, a 36% reduction. Draining, rinsing for about 10 seconds and draining again lowered it to 295 mg, a 41% reduction.

In that dataset, rinsing after draining removed an additional 26 mg per serving. Draining therefore did most of the work, while rinsing provided a smaller extra reduction.

Not every can needs the same treatment

Canned beans may be regular-sodium, reduced-sodium or no-salt-added. A no-salt-added can can start very low in sodium, so rinsing it for nutrition offers little advantage. Reading the actual Nutrition Facts panel is more useful than applying one rule to every can.

Does rinsing wash away nutrients?

The liquid contains soluble compounds: sodium, potassium, some folate and other B vitamins, carbohydrates and small amounts of protein. Draining and rinsing removes a portion of these, but most protein and fiber stay in the bean.

If the goal is to remove several hundred milligrams of sodium, the modest loss of water-soluble nutrients does not make rinsing nutritionally pointless.

Chickpea liquid can be useful

Chickpea cooking or canning liquid is aquafaba. It contains soluble proteins, carbohydrates and saponins that help it foam and emulsify. If a recipe uses aquafaba as an egg-white-style culinary ingredient, saving the liquid makes sense.

What about soups and hummus?

In soup or chili, some packing liquid can add body. In hummus, a little aquafaba can loosen the texture. If the can is salty, rinse the beans and add water or a lower-sodium liquid instead to control the final sodium level.

Bottom line

Rinsing canned beans is optional: do it when you want less sodium, less packing-liquid flavor or a cleaner surface. If the can is no-salt-added or you need the liquid for a recipe, there is no universal nutritional reason to discard it.

faq.question: Does rinsing canned beans reduce sodium?
faq.answer: Yes. In one multi-brand study, draining reduced sodium by 36% on average and draining plus rinsing reduced it by 41%.

faq.question: Is chickpea can liquid safe to use?
faq.answer: Yes. Aquafaba is edible and is used for its foaming and emulsifying properties.

faq.question: Do no-salt-added beans need rinsing?
faq.answer: Not for sodium reduction. You may still rinse them for texture or flavor.
